title: African Literature in English
subtitle: Narrativ versjon
description: A story of how African writers seized the pen from outsiders -- from Achebe's proverb-rich Igbo world to Ngugi's defiant turn to his mother tongue to Adichie's warning about the single story.
competenceGoals: analyze and interpret literary texts from the English-speaking world in a historical and cultural context
discuss how texts from the English-speaking world relate to the historical period in which they were written

content.content:
## Telling Africa's Own Stories

Africa is a continent of 54 nations, hundreds of languages, and extraordinarily diverse cultures. Yet for much of the twentieth century, African stories were told primarily by outsiders -- European missionaries, colonial administrators, and Western journalists. When Africans began writing their own stories in English, they did not merely add new titles to the global bookshelf. They fundamentally challenged the way the world understood an entire continent.

**African literature in English** refers to literary works written in English by authors from the African continent -- a subset of the broader category that also includes works in French, Portuguese, Arabic, Swahili, and many African languages. English became a literary language in Africa as a direct result of British colonialism, the first major works appeared in the 1950s, and the tradition now spans multiple generations and has produced several Nobel and Booker Prize winners. Its major literary centres include Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa, Ghana, Zimbabwe, and Sierra Leone. In this chapter we will trace its development through three towering figures -- Chinua Achebe, Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o, and Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie.

## Achebe and the Birth of Modern African Literature

Chinua Achebe's *Things Fall Apart* (1958) is widely regarded as the founding text of modern African literature in English. Set in a fictional Igbo village at the end of the nineteenth century, it tells the story of Okonkwo, a proud warrior whose world is shattered by the arrival of British missionaries and colonial administrators.

Why does it matter so much? Before Achebe, the dominant Western literary image of Africa was Joseph Conrad's *Heart of Darkness* (1899), which depicted Africa as a place of savagery -- a backdrop for European moral crises rather than a land of real people with real cultures. Achebe responded directly. His novel presents pre-colonial Igbo society as complex, sophisticated, and governed by elaborate systems of law, religion, and social organization. He achieved this through several techniques. He wove **Igbo proverbs** throughout the English text -- as his narrator says, "Among the Igbo, the art of conversation is regarded very highly, and proverbs are the palm-oil with which words are eaten." Proverbs like "A toad does not run in the daytime for nothing" establish the cultural richness of Igbo society, create a narrative voice that sounds African rather than British, and challenge the colonial assumption that cultures without written literature are "primitive." He used a **tragic structure**, with Okonkwo as a flawed hero whose rigidity leads to his downfall, and rich **cultural detail** that presents Igbo life as fully realized. And he showed the **colonial encounter** from the African perspective. Achebe went on to write four more novels and to argue, in his essay "An Image of Africa" (1977), that Conrad's *Heart of Darkness* is fundamentally racist.

exercise.task: Test yourself on Achebe and Things Fall Apart:

options.text: placeholder

questions.task: What was Achebe responding to in 'Things Fall Apart'?

options.text: Western images of Africa as savage, like Conrad's 'Heart of Darkness'
The poetry of Derek Walcott
The work of Salman Rushdie
An attack on the English language

questions.solution: Achebe responded to the dominant Western image of Africa as a place of savagery (epitomised by Conrad's Heart of Darkness), presenting Igbo society as complex and sophisticated.

questions.task: How does Achebe use Igbo proverbs in his English novel?

options.text: To confuse Western readers
To show the richness of Igbo oral culture and create an African narrative voice
To prove Igbo culture was primitive
To imitate British literature exactly

questions.solution: Achebe weaves Igbo proverbs throughout the English text -- 'proverbs are the palm-oil with which words are eaten' -- demonstrating the sophistication of Igbo oral tradition and creating an African voice.

questions.task: In his essay 'An Image of Africa' (1977), what did Achebe argue about Conrad's 'Heart of Darkness'?

options.text: That it is the greatest novel ever written
That it accurately portrays Africa
That it is fundamentally racist
That it should be taught as a model

questions.solution: Achebe's influential essay argued that Conrad's Heart of Darkness is fundamentally racist and should not be celebrated uncritically as a great work of literature.

questions.task: Why is 'Things Fall Apart' considered so important?

options.text: It was the first novel ever written
It was written in Igbo, not English
It praised British colonialism
It is widely regarded as the founding text of modern African literature in English

questions.solution: Things Fall Apart (1958) is widely seen as the founding text of modern African literature in English, proving African stories could be told powerfully in a reshaped English.

content.content:
## Ngũgĩ's Defiance and Adichie's New Generation

The Kenyan writer **Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o** (born 1938) is one of the most influential African intellectuals of the twentieth century. His early novels, including *Weep Not, Child* (1964), were written in English and dealt with Kenya's struggle for independence from British rule. But in 1986 he published *Decolonising the Mind*, arguing that language is the most powerful instrument of cultural imperialism, and announced he would no longer write fiction in English -- choosing instead his mother tongue, Gikuyu. His argument was that language carries culture, that adopting the colonizer's language means adopting the colonizer's worldview, that colonial education deliberately destroyed African children's connection to their own languages, and that writing in African languages is an act of resistance. His position sparked intense debate: critics argued it limited his readership and that English could be reshaped (Achebe's view), while supporters argued he was right to prioritize African audiences. Ngũgĩ was even imprisoned by the Kenyan government in 1977 for his politically engaged work.

**Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie** (born 1977) represents the contemporary generation of African writers who have achieved global stardom. Born in Nigeria and educated in both Nigeria and the United States, she writes with equal authority about African and American settings. *Half of a Yellow Sun* (2006), set during the Nigerian Civil War (the Biafran War), tells the conflict through five intersecting lives, recovering a suppressed history. *Americanah* (2013) follows Ifemelu, a young Nigerian woman who moves to the United States and discovers she is "Black" for the first time -- in Nigeria she was Igbo and middle-class, but race as Americans understand it was not a defining category. Her 2009 TED Talk **"The Danger of a Single Story"** has become one of the most-watched ever. The **single story** is a concept she articulated: a single story is not necessarily untrue, but it is *incomplete*; when we hear only one story about a people, we reduce them to it. As she puts it, "The problem with stereotypes is not that they are untrue, but that they are incomplete" -- and power determines which stories get told. Literature offering multiple perspectives is the antidote.

exercise.task: Test yourself on Ngugi and Adichie:

options.text: placeholder

questions.task: What did Ngugi wa Thiong'o announce in 'Decolonising the Mind' (1986)?

options.text: That he would write fiction in Gikuyu, his mother tongue, rather than English
That all writers should use only English
That he would stop writing forever
That English is the best language for everyone

questions.solution: In Decolonising the Mind, Ngugi argued language is the key instrument of cultural imperialism and announced he would write in Gikuyu, not English, as an act of decolonization.

questions.task: In 'Americanah', what does Ifemelu discover when she moves to the United States?

options.text: That race does not matter anywhere
That she is seen as 'Black' for the first time -- a category that did not define her in Nigeria
That America has no racism
That Nigeria and America are identical

questions.solution: Americanah explores how Ifemelu becomes 'Black' in America, whereas in Nigeria she was Igbo and middle-class -- showing how race and identity shift with geography.

questions.task: What is the core idea of Adichie's 'single story'?

options.text: A single story is always a lie
There should only ever be one story
A single story is incomplete, and hearing only one reduces a people to it
Stories have no effect on perception

questions.solution: The single story is not necessarily untrue but incomplete. Hearing only one story about a people reduces them to it -- 'the problem with stereotypes is not that they are untrue, but that they are incomplete.'

questions.task: Why was Ngugi wa Thiong'o imprisoned in 1977?

options.text: For writing in English
For refusing to write at all
For praising British rule
For his politically engaged work

questions.solution: Ngugi was imprisoned by the Kenyan government in 1977 for his politically engaged work, an experience documented in his prison memoir Detained.

content.content:
## Summary

African literature in English has grown from Achebe's pioneering work in the 1950s into one of the world's most vibrant literary traditions. **Chinua Achebe** established it, proving in *Things Fall Apart* that African stories could be told powerfully in a reshaped English carrying Igbo proverbs and perspectives, while responding to racist Western images like Conrad's *Heart of Darkness*. **Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o** challenged the tradition, arguing in *Decolonising the Mind* that true decolonization requires writing in African languages, and switching to Gikuyu. **Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie** represents the new generation, writing about both African and Western settings and warning, in "The Danger of a Single Story," that reducing a people to one incomplete narrative is a form of oppression. Central themes include colonialism's impact, the politics of language, the immigrant experience, and the need for diverse representation.
